interviewQuestions.question: How do you balance YAGNI against designing for extensibility?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I don't pick a side — the question is testing whether I can hold the actual tension and draw a line, so I state it directly: YAGNI kills pure speculation, but a cheap seam for a known, near-term variation is worth building even before a second use case exists.

Concretely, a one-method `PaymentGateway` interface with a single `StripeGateway` implementation costs almost nothing today — I was going to write that class anyway — and costs almost nothing to delete if a second provider never shows up. A generic plugin framework with dynamic dispatch and hook registration, built before any second provider is real, is the opposite: hundreds of lines of machinery based on a guess, and when the real second case does arrive, it often needs something the guess didn't anticipate.

My test: price the build cost and the cost of being wrong. If both are low, build the seam now. If either is high, wait for a real second example.

**Testing:** whether you can hold two correct-sounding principles in tension and give a real, checkable line between them instead of picking one absolutely.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Drawing the line between YAGNI and extensibility

interviewQuestions.question: Your PM says 'we'll definitely need X in Q3' — does that change how you'd apply YAGNI here?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Yes, and I'd say so directly: a committed, dated requirement isn't speculation anymore, so YAGNI doesn't apply to it the same way. But I'd also push back gently on "definitely" — I'd ask whether that's a signed roadmap commitment or a hope, since the two deserve very different levels of investment.

If it's genuinely committed, I'd build a seam sized specifically to that Q3 requirement — not a generic framework sized for an unknown range of hypothetical future requirements I'm still guessing at. The scope of what I build should match the scope of what's actually confirmed, not expand to cover every future possibility just because one future need is now real.

I'd also flag that "Q3" gives me a natural checkpoint: if the requirement slips or changes shape before then, I want to revisit the seam rather than have already over-built around today's guess of what Q3 needs.

**Testing:** whether you can update your YAGNI judgment based on real evidence without over-correcting into building far more than the evidence actually supports.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: When a future need becomes committed

interviewQuestions.question: How do you tell the difference between 'premature extensibility' and 'the extension point that would've saved us a rewrite,' looking back after the fact?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The tell, in hindsight, is usually how cheaply the actual need could have been retrofitted versus how much of the codebase had to change once it showed up. If a genuinely new requirement lands and adding it takes one new class implementing an existing interface, because the seam was already there as a single method call through an abstraction, that seam was cheap to build and would have looked justified even before you knew you'd need it. That's the "would've saved us a rewrite" case.

If instead the extension point you built years ago sits unused, wraps something that never varied, and its generic parameters get in the way every time someone reads the code, that's premature extensibility, and the giveaway is that removing it today would be a net simplification, not a loss of capability.

A concrete example: a payments module built with a `PaymentStrategy` interface from day one, even with only one processor, turned out cheap, one interface, one implementation, near-zero overhead, and paid off eighteen months later when a second processor was added in one afternoon. Contrast that with a `GenericEventBus` built "in case we need pub/sub" that no feature ever used, it added indirection to every event-emitting call site for years before someone finally deleted it.

The retrospective rule I use: extensibility that costs almost nothing when unused is worth keeping speculatively; extensibility that adds real complexity to every caller needs actual evidence of a second use case first.
**Testing:** whether you can evaluate a past architectural bet honestly instead of rationalizing whichever choice you made.
